t.2.32.1: Then the descendant of Ikṣvāku, tormented here by his promise, sighed deeply with tears and spoke these words to Sumantra again and again.
t.2.32.2: O charioteer, let an army of four divisions, amply furnished with jewels, be quickly made ready to follow Rāghava.
t.2.32.3: Let graceful courtesans and merchants of great wealth, well arrayed, adorn the prince's army.
t.2.32.4: Those who depend on him for their living, and those in whose company he delights because of their valour, give them gifts of many kinds and appoint them too to this task.
t.2.32.5: Slaying deer and elephants, drinking the honey of the forest, and gazing upon rivers of many kinds, he will not remember the kingdom.
t.2.32.6: Whatever granary and whatever treasury of mine there may be, let both of them follow Rāma as he dwells in the desolate forest.
t.2.32.7: Performing sacrifices in holy places and bestowing fitting sacrificial fees, and keeping company with the seers, he will dwell happily in the forest.
t.2.32.8: And mighty-armed Bharata will protect Ayodhyā; let the glorious Rāma, for his part, be furnished with every object of desire.
t.2.32.10: Dejected and alarmed, Kaikeyī spoke these words: "O good man, Bharata will not accept a kingdom emptied of its people, utterly tasteless and void, like wine whose cream has been drunk off."
t.2.32.9: As Kākutstha spoke in this way, fear came upon Kaikeyī; her mouth went dry, and her voice was choked.
t.2.32.11: While Kaikeyī, having cast off all shame, was speaking these most cruel words, King Daśaratha said to the long-eyed woman: "Why do you torment me, who am already bearing the load, after yoking me to the burden laid upon me?"
t.2.32.13: Thus addressed, King Daśaratha said only, "Shame!" All the people were ashamed, but she did not perceive it.
t.2.32.12: Kaikeyī, doubly enraged, spoke these words to the king: "In your very own lineage Sagara cast out his eldest son, the one known as Asamañja; in the same way this one ought to go."
t.2.32.14: Then an aged chief minister, Siddhārtha by name, upright and highly esteemed by the king, spoke these words to Kaikeyī.
t.2.32.15: Asamañja, in his sport, would seize children on the road and fling them into the waters of the Sarayū, and the evil-minded one took delight in that.
t.2.32.16: Seeing him, all the citizens in their anger said to the king: "Choose either Asamañja alone or us, O increaser of the kingdom!"
t.2.32.17: Then the king said to them, "What is the cause of this fear?" And the subjects, thus questioned by the king, spoke these words.
t.2.32.18: In his sport, this one, his mind deranged, throws our young sons into the Sarayū out of sheer folly and takes boundless delight in it.
t.2.32.19: Having heard the words of those subjects, O lord of men, he abandoned that harmful son out of a desire to do what was pleasing to them.
t.2.32.20: Thus did the most righteous King Sagara abandon his son. What sin has Rāma committed, that he is obstructed in this way?
t.2.32.21: Having heard Siddhārtha's words, the king, his voice grown ever more weary, spoke thus to Kaikeyī in a voice stricken with grief.
t.2.32.22: Today I shall follow Rāma, abandoning the kingdom, comfort and wealth. Together with the king and with Bharata, may you enjoy the kingdom as you please for a long time.
